intro: Frank Lévy’s performance comes from Musopen’s Set Chopin Free project. On one piano, melody and accompaniment share the same decaying sound: follow how the decorated line remains distinct from the recurring bass pattern.
question: How does a pianist keep the decorated melody above the accompaniment?

cues.title: One piano, two layers
cues.text: Lévy’s piano carries both the decorated melody and the repeated accompaniment. Follow the upper line across its gaps while the lower pattern provides continuity.
cues.evidence: The source identifies Lévy playing solo piano. The melody and accompaniment are written features described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nocturnes,_Op._9_(Chopin). This is a whole-performance listening point.

cues.title: An early rise and release
cues.text: In the opening spans, the phrase grows and then relaxes into quieter sound. Listen for whether the melodic line remains connected as individual piano attacks decay.
cues.evidence: The report shows −16.2 dB at 0:45, then −22.4 dB at 0:55, with a boundary at 0:50. No individual pedal action is inferred.

cues.title: More attacks within the line
cues.text: Through this stretch, more notes fit inside the melodic gesture. Keep following the phrase above the accompaniment rather than treating each small attack as a new accent.
cues.evidence: Onset density rises from 1.6 per second at 1:20 to 3.8 at 1:35, then falls to 2.0 at 1:45. The score’s ornamented melody supplies the listening focus; exact ornaments are not identified.

cues.title: The later expansion
cues.text: A later ascent brings a stronger swell, followed by a retreat. Listen across its crest to the quieter space beyond it, keeping the same melodic thread in mind.
cues.evidence: The 2:14 boundary precedes the rise to −10.7 dB at 2:25; level then retreats to −17.9 dB at 2:50 and −24.6 dB at 3:00.

cues.title: Quietness inside the phrase
cues.text: This quieter stretch does not finish the piece. Hear how the piano reconnects the line after a reduction in weight before the later closing build.
cues.evidence: The 2:52 boundary is followed by −24.6 dB at 3:00, then renewed activity at 3:05. The largest closing crest is still ahead at 3:30–3:45.

cues.title: The late broad crest
cues.text: The closing build reaches Lévy’s strongest recorded span, then gives way to lighter, quicker attacks. Compare the broad rise with the way its energy is released.
cues.evidence: The 3:30–3:45 windows dominate the report’s highest levels. At 3:50–3:55 level falls while onset density rises to 4.8–5.2 per second; no specific cadenza note is timed.

cues.title: Cadence before silence
cues.text: The last phrase leaves time for the piano’s resonance to decay. Listen beyond the renewed final attacks instead of stopping at the apparent point of arrival.
cues.evidence: The strongest boundary is 4:08; level briefly rises at 4:10, then falls through 4:15–4:30. No attacks are detected in the final three windows.

transitions.title: The phrase gathers fresh weight
transitions.how: The recurring melodic design acquires another rise in weight. The melody remains above the accompaniment; the marker describes the recorded expansion rather than a new formal theme.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 2:14; relative level rises to the high 2:25–2:30 windows.

transitions.title: Quiet playing opens the last ascent
transitions.how: The quieter late passage leads into the last substantial ascent. Its crest releases into a denser succession of lighter attacks before the final cadence.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 3:26 precedes the highest 3:30–3:45 windows; the following onset-density rise at 3:50–3:55 supports the release description.

transitions.title: The remaining attacks leave resonance
transitions.how: The ornamental release gives way to the final cadential sound. Fresh attacks briefly renew the piano’s resonance before it is left to decay.
transitions.evidence: The written piano work closes in E♭ major; the 4:08 boundary and renewed 4:10 level precede a sustained decay. This is not an exact bar alignment.

facts: Wojciech Żywny; Józef Elsner at Warsaw’s Main School of Music, 1826–29
Warsaw until 1830; Paris from 1831; summers at George Sand’s house in Nohant
Teaching, publication and selected performances, more often in salons than large public halls
Almost entirely centred on the piano: études, mazurkas, polonaises, nocturnes, preludes, ballades, scherzos, sonatas and concertos
composer.background:
Chopin was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810, to a French-born father, Nicolas, and a Polish mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska. The family soon moved to Warsaw, where Nicolas taught French. The name Fryderyk belongs to his Polish life; Frédéric became usual in France. His family observed his birthday on 1 March, although the baptismal record gives 22 February. Piano lessons with Wojciech Żywny introduced Bach and Mozart alongside the fashionable repertory of the day. As a child he composed polonaises and played in aristocratic houses, but his later musical education extended beyond the cultivation of a prodigy.

Józef Elsner taught him harmony and composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music from 1826 to 1829. Chopin heard Italian opera, encountered Polish vernacular music during visits outside the capital and learned the working forms of the virtuoso concerto. The F minor Concerto was composed before the E minor, despite their eventual numbering as Nos. 2 and 1. Both preserve an extended orchestral opening, but once the piano enters, its vocal line and ornament determine the movement’s scale. The slow movements belong as much to operatic singing as to the display repertory of a concert pianist.
composer.born: 1 March 1810, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He made the piano sing through ornament, contrapuntal voice-leading and the unstable accents of Polish dance.
